newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda says 1997/98 earnings in line with forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Mazda says 1997/98 earnings in line with forecasts.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp said on Friday that its parent earnings so far this business year have been in line with its earlier forecasts.
Mazda president Henry Wallace told reporters in Hiroshima, western Japan, that the firm's worldwide sales and production this business year had been as planned.
"Our (earnings) projections have not been changed." he said.

In late May, Mazda, Japan's fifth biggest carmaker, predicted that its parent current profit would rise 43.9 percent to 20 billion yen in the current business year to March 31 1998, helped by sales of new models it plans to launch later this year.
Wallace said Mazda was trying to increase its production at its Hofu plant in western Japan, and in order to do so it would start producing a new car model at the plant next year.
Asked to comment on a media report which said the company was aiming for full operations at Hofu next year, he said:
"It's unlikely that we will get to that level so quickly -- that's too ambitious."

Operation rates at the plant, which is capable of producing 390,000 cars a year, have averaged just 40 percent a year in recent years. Mazda has said that it expects the rate to be 50 percent in the six-month period to September 30 and 60 percent in the second half of the current business year.
It posted a parent current profit of 13.90 billion yen in 1996/97, sharply higher from 1.23 billion yen a year earlier.
Wallace said that although there was still a lot to be done to improve profitability at Mazda, the structure for doing so was in place and business was growing.
"The sun is not shining, but it is just coming out," he said.
He said he hoped that sales in the United States had bottomed out after the firm managed strong sales there in June.
However he did not say when Mazda's loss-making U.S. operations might become profitable.
Wallace, a Briton, took the wheel at Mazda in June last year after Ford Motor Co raised its stake in the Japanese carmaker to a third in order to gain management control.
He is first foreigner to head a major Japanese company and has been charged with turning around the firm's troubled finances.
